analogy.p: Imagine a squash court with lots of tennis balls bouncing around at random. Each ball hitting the walls gives them a tiny push, and billions of tiny pushes add up to a steady push, which is gas pressure. If the court shrinks (a smaller volume), the balls hit the walls more often so the push is bigger; if the balls move faster (higher temperature), every hit is harder and more frequent. The analogy breaks down because real gas particles are invisible, vastly more numerous and collide with each other as well as the walls, and balls on a court lose energy while ideal gas particles do not.
analogy.t: A hall full of bouncing tennis balls

bullets: **Random motion**: each particle moves in a straight line until it collides, then bounces off in a new direction, so the motion has no pattern.
**Large gaps**: gas particles are about ten times further apart than particles in a solid or liquid, which is why gases have a very low density.
**Negligible forces**: the forces of attraction between particles are very weak, so particles move independently.
**Speed**: particles move at hundreds of metres per second at room temperature, with a range of speeds; temperature is linked to the average kinetic energy.
**Fixed mass**: when a gas is in a sealed container the number of particles (the mass of gas) does not change, which is the assumption in all pressure–volume questions.
**Link to other topics**: this is the same particle model used for states of matter, density and specific latent heat.
core.h: What a gas is like at particle level
core.p: In a **gas** the particles are far apart, have almost no forces of attraction between them and move quickly in **random** directions. They are constantly colliding with each other and with the walls of whatever contains them. Because the particles move freely, a gas has no fixed shape and fills the whole container, and it can be compressed because there is so much empty space between the particles. The particle model is what lets us explain pressure without needing to see anything.

bullets: Pressure comes from collisions with the walls, not from particles pushing each other.
The force from each collision is at right angles to the surface because the wall is what the particle bounces off.
Because the number of collisions is huge and the motion is random, the pressure is the same in every direction and is steady.
Pressure = force ÷ area, so the same force on a smaller area gives a larger pressure.
The unit of pressure is the **pascal (Pa)**; 1 Pa = 1 N/m². Gas pressures are often given in kilopascals (kPa): 1 kPa = 1000 Pa.
Model phrase for mark schemes: 'the particles collide with the walls of the container and exert a force at right angles to the wall; the pressure is the force per unit area'.
core.p: The **pressure** of a gas is produced by its particles colliding with the walls of the container (or with any surface in the gas). Each time a particle hits a wall it bounces back, so its momentum changes, which means the wall exerts a force on the particle and, by Newton's third law, the particle exerts a force on the wall. One collision is tiny, but billions of collisions every second add up to a steady **net force** on the wall. This resultant force acts at **right angles (90°)** to the wall, and pressure is that force spread over the area of the wall.

bullets: More particles in the same volume means more collisions per second, so a higher pressure.
Faster particles hit the wall more often and with a greater change of momentum, so a greater force per collision.
A smaller volume squeezes the same particles into less space, so they hit the walls more often.
A larger volume lets particles travel further between collisions, so collisions are less frequent and pressure falls.
Temperature and volume can both change at once; always say which is being kept constant.
Atmospheric pressure is also caused by gas particles hitting surfaces; it decreases with height because there are fewer air particles above.
core.h: What affects the pressure of a gas
core.p: The pressure depends on how often particles hit the walls and how hard they hit. Anything that increases the **frequency of collisions** or the **force of each collision** increases the pressure. For a fixed mass of gas, the two things you can change are the temperature and the volume of the container. Learn to link each change to collisions every time; stating only 'the pressure goes up' earns no marks.

bullets: Temperature of a gas is linked to the average kinetic energy of its particles.
Higher temperature → faster particles → more frequent collisions AND harder collisions.
Volume must be constant for this effect; if the container can expand (like a balloon) the volume increases instead.
Cooling does the reverse: slower particles, fewer and gentler collisions, lower pressure (a car tyre pressure falls on a cold morning).
The temperature must be in kelvin for any proportionality statements; at GCSE you only need the qualitative link.
Typical exam wording: 'the particles gain kinetic energy, move faster, collide with the walls more often and with greater force, so pressure increases'.
core.h: Temperature and pressure at constant volume
core.p: If a fixed mass of gas is heated in a container that cannot expand, its pressure rises. Heating transfers energy to the particles' **kinetic energy stores**, so they move faster on average. Faster particles collide with the walls more frequently and each collision has a larger change in momentum, so the force on the wall is bigger. As the area of the wall is the same, the pressure increases. This is why a sealed can or aerosol must not be put in a fire.

bullets: Decrease volume → particles closer together → hit walls more often (per unit area) → pressure increases.
Increase volume → particles further apart → hit walls less often → pressure decreases.
The particles' average speed is unchanged because the temperature is constant, so each collision is as forceful as before.
The pressure is **inversely proportional** to the volume for a fixed mass of gas at constant temperature.
Double the volume → pressure halves; halve the volume → pressure doubles.
Real example: pulling the plunger of a sealed syringe out lowers the pressure so the gas is 'sucked' to fill the space.
core.h: Volume and pressure at constant temperature (Boyle's law idea)
core.p: For a fixed mass of gas at constant temperature, decreasing the volume increases the pressure and increasing the volume decreases the pressure. Particles move at the same average speed, so the force of each collision is the same, but in a smaller container they travel shorter distances between collisions with the walls and so hit them more often. **Higher Tier**: you must be able to explain this clearly in terms of collision frequency, and say that the force per collision does not change because the temperature (average speed) has not changed.

bullets: Equation: pressure × volume = constant, or p₁V₁ = p₂V₂.
Rearranged: p₂ = (p₁ × V₁) ÷ V₂ and V₂ = (p₁ × V₁) ÷ p₂.
Units: pressure in pascals (Pa), volume in cubic metres (m³), and p × V therefore in joules (J) in SI units.
Units can stay as kPa and cm³ if both sides use the same ones, because the conversion factors cancel.
Check your answer: if volume goes down, pressure must go up, and the product p × V should match on both sides.
Graph of p against V is a curve (a hyperbola) that never touches the axes; a graph of p against 1/V is a straight line through the origin.
core.p: For a **fixed mass of gas at constant temperature**, the product of pressure and volume stays the same: **pressure × volume = constant**. This means that if the pressure or volume changes from a starting pair of values (p₁ and V₁) to new values (p₂ and V₂), then p₁ × V₁ = p₂ × V₂. The equation is on the physics-only list and you will need to use it in calculations, remembering that the temperature must not change and the gas must not escape. Pressure may be in Pa or kPa and volume in m³ or cm³, as long as you use the same units for the initial and final values.

bullets: Step 1: write down p₁, V₁ and the one unknown (p₂ or V₂).
Step 2: write p₁ × V₁ = p₂ × V₂.
Step 3: rearrange for the unknown, for example p₂ = p₁V₁ ÷ V₂.
Step 4: substitute, keeping units consistent, and calculate.
Step 5: sense check – smaller volume must give bigger pressure.
Step 6: give the unit; if you converted, convert back to the unit the question asks for.
core.h: Working with the p–V relationship: method
core.p: Calculations on this topic are often 3 or 4 marks and follow a set pattern. You should always write the equation first, substitute the values in the same units, and rearrange for the unknown. Showing p₁V₁ = p₂V₂ clearly earns the method mark even if the arithmetic goes wrong. The most common errors are mixing units (kPa with Pa, or cm³ with m³) and using the temperature when it has changed.

bullets: Work done on a gas = force × distance moved in the direction of the force.
Energy transferred by work increases the internal energy of the gas, so the temperature rises.
Example: the barrel of a bicycle pump becomes warm when you pump quickly.
If the compression is slow, the gas has time to transfer energy to the surroundings by heating, so the temperature rise is smaller.
Rapid expansion is the opposite: the gas does work on its surroundings, loses internal energy and cools (an aerosol can feels cold when sprayed).
Link to energy topic: energy is transferred (by work), not created, and total energy is conserved.
core.h: Doing work on a gas: compression and temperature
core.p: When a gas is compressed quickly, **work is done on the gas** because a force moves the piston through a distance. This energy transferred by work is stored in the gas, increasing its **internal energy** (the total kinetic and potential energy of its particles). In a gas, nearly all of this increase appears as extra kinetic energy of the particles, so the **temperature of the gas increases**. The particles bounce off the moving piston faster than they arrived, like a ball hitting a bat that moves towards it, which is the particle-level reason for the gain in speed.

bullets: Moving piston + colliding particle = particle leaves faster than it arrived.
Faster particles = higher average kinetic energy = higher temperature.
The pressure rises for two reasons: smaller volume (more frequent collisions) and higher speed (harder collisions).
This is why the pressure rise on fast compression is larger than predicted by p₁V₁ = p₂V₂ (which assumes constant temperature).
In an exam, say 'work is done on the gas' rather than 'heat is added'.
Reverse process: when gas expands against a piston, particles rebound slower and the gas cools.
core.h: Particle explanation of the temperature rise during compression (Higher tier)
core.p: As the piston moves into the gas, a particle that collides with it rebounds with greater speed than it had before, because the surface it hits is moving towards it. Over many collisions the average speed of the gas particles increases, meaning the average **kinetic energy increases**, which is the temperature rise. This is why compressing gas can cause both a volume decrease and a temperature increase together, so pV is only constant when the temperature is constant. Exam answers should connect energy transfer by work, the increase in internal energy and the faster particles.

bullets: **Bicycle pump**: pushing in the plunger reduces volume so pressure rises until the tyre valve opens; the barrel also warms because work is done on the gas.
**Sealed syringe**: pushing the plunger in compresses the trapped air; the push is harder as pressure rises because pressure is inversely proportional to volume.
**Car tyre**: pressure is lower in cold weather because the air particles move more slowly and collide less often and less forcefully.
**Aerosol or gas canister in a fire**: temperature rises, pressure rises at constant volume and the can may explode.
**Weather balloon**: rises into lower atmospheric pressure so the gas inside expands (volume increases) and the balloon grows.
**Scuba diver**: pressure underwater is higher, so air spaces in the body are compressed (volume decreases).
core.p: Many exam questions set these ideas in a context such as syringes, tyres, balloons or diving. You need to identify what is constant (mass, temperature, volume) and then apply the particle explanation to the situation. Approach each context by asking: has the volume changed, has the temperature changed, has any gas been added or removed? Then choose the correct explanation.

bullets: Table check: multiply p × V for every row; a constant product shows inverse proportionality.
Curve of p against V falls steeply at small V, then flattens, and never reaches zero.
Straight line of p against 1/V through the origin shows p ∝ 1/V.
When reading from a graph, state the units on the axes in your answer.
If asked to 'describe the pattern', say: as the volume increases the pressure decreases, and when the volume doubles the pressure halves.
Plot with the independent variable (the one you change, usually volume) on the x-axis.
core.p: You may be given a table of pressure and volume values or a graph and asked to show that pressure is inversely proportional to volume, or to find a missing value. In a table, calculate p × V for each row; if the values are all the same (within rounding) the relationship holds. On a graph of p against V you should be able to read values and recognise the curved shape, and on a p against 1/V graph you should recognise the straight line through the origin. Always use a ruler for lines and read from the graph carefully at the gridlines.

bullets: Links to **density**: compressing the gas reduces the volume while the mass stays the same, so the density increases.
Links to **internal energy**: temperature and state changes alter the internal energy; compression does work on the gas.
Links to **forces and pressure** (Physics only): pressure = force ÷ area applies to gases as well as solids and liquids.
Links to **energy transfers**: energy in a pump is transferred by work, then by heating to the surroundings.
Links to **specific heat capacity**: a temperature rise needs a certain energy input.
In experiments with a syringe and pressure gauge, a control is keeping the temperature constant by moving the plunger slowly.
core.h: Linking ideas and common exam contexts
core.p: This topic links the particle model, energy, forces and graphs, so exam questions combine them. For example, a question may start with a gas being compressed and ask for the change in temperature, then the change in pressure, then a calculation. Be systematic and answer each part in terms of what the particles are doing. Keeping the key assumptions (constant mass, constant temperature) in view will stop you from applying the equation wrongly.

exam: Command words: 'Explain' needs a reason linked to particles (collisions, speed, frequency); 'Describe' needs the pattern only; 'Calculate' needs equation, substitution and unit.
1 mark: a definition such as 'gas pressure is caused by particles colliding with the walls of the container'.
2 marks: a statement of change plus reason, e.g. 'the particles move faster (1) so they collide with the walls more often and with greater force (1)'.
3 to 4 mark explanations: use a chain: change → particle effect → collision effect → pressure effect. Always mention 'collide with the walls' and 'force'.
For constant-temperature volume questions, include 'the average speed/kinetic energy of the particles does not change, but the collisions are more frequent'.
Calculations: write p₁V₁ = p₂V₂, substitute, rearrange, answer with unit. Show the working because a wrong answer can still score method marks.
Keep units consistent: either both pressures in kPa and both volumes in cm³, or convert to Pa and m³.
For 'why does the pump get warm' say: work is done on the gas, increasing its internal energy, so the temperature rises.
Graph questions: for p against V say 'curve, as volume increases pressure decreases', for p against 1/V say 'straight line through the origin shows inverse proportionality'.
Required experiment-style questions: say the temperature is kept constant by moving the plunger slowly and waiting, and use a gauge to read pressure.

mistakes.r: The pressure is caused by particles colliding with the walls of the container and exerting a force at right angles to the wall.
mistakes.w: The particles push against each other, which makes the pressure.

mistakes.r: The particles do not expand; they gain kinetic energy and move faster, so they collide with the walls more often and with greater force.
mistakes.w: The particles get hotter so they expand.

mistakes.r: At constant temperature the particles' speed is unchanged, so collisions are not harder; they are more frequent because the particles are closer to the walls.
mistakes.w: Pressure increases because there is less space, so the particles hit the walls harder (at constant temperature).

mistakes.r: At constant temperature pressure is inversely proportional to volume; pressure × volume is constant.
Use the same units on both sides, or convert to Pa and m³ first; then convert back to the unit asked for.
mistakes.w: Using p₁V₁ = p₂V₂ with one value in kPa and another in Pa.

mistakes.r: Work is done on the gas, increasing its internal energy and temperature (friction contributes a little, but compression is the main reason).
mistakes.w: The pump gets hot because of friction only.

mistakes.r: Energy is transferred by work being done on the gas, not by heating.
mistakes.w: The gas gets heat added when it is compressed.

mistakes.r: In a small gas container the pressure is the same everywhere; gas pressure arises from random collisions, not weight.
mistakes.w: The pressure is bigger at the bottom of a container because of gravity pulling particles down (for a gas in a box).

mistakes.r: The mass stays the same; the density increases because the same mass occupies a smaller volume.
mistakes.w: Mass of gas goes up when it is compressed.

summary: You must know that gas pressure is caused by particles colliding with the container walls, how temperature and volume change that pressure, and (physics only) that for a fixed mass of gas at constant temperature pressure × volume is constant. You must also explain how doing work on a gas (for example compressing it) raises its temperature. It matters because it explains bike pumps, aerosols, tyres and why sealed containers can burst when heated.

terms.d: The force per unit area exerted by gas particles colliding with the walls of their container, acting at right angles to the wall.
The unit of pressure; 1 pascal is a force of 1 newton acting on 1 square metre (1 N/m²).
Movement of particles in constantly changing directions with no pattern.
The overall (resultant) force produced by many particle collisions; it acts at right angles to the surface.
The energy stored in a moving object or particle, depending on its mass and speed.
The total kinetic energy and potential energy of all the particles in a system.
Energy transferred when a force moves an object through a distance; work done = force × distance moved in the direction of the force.
A sealed amount of gas where no particles enter or leave, so the number of particles is constant.
Condition where the average kinetic energy of the particles does not change, so the average particle speed is unchanged.
Two quantities where one halves when the other doubles; their product is constant.
For a fixed mass of gas at constant temperature, pressure × volume = constant.
Reducing the volume of a gas by pushing on it, which increases its pressure.
The number of collisions of particles with the wall per second.
The lowest possible temperature, 0 K (−273 °C), where particles have minimum kinetic energy.
The pressure caused by the weight of air above a surface, caused by air particles colliding with it.

worked.q: A syringe traps 120 cm³ of air at a pressure of 100 kPa. The plunger is pushed in slowly so the volume becomes 40 cm³. The temperature stays constant. Calculate the new pressure. (3 marks)
steps: p₁ = 100 kPa, V₁ = 120 cm³, V₂ = 40 cm³
Sense check: volume decreased to a third, so pressure should triple: 3 × 100 = 300 kPa ✓

worked.q: A fixed mass of gas has a pressure of 150 kPa and a volume of 2.0 m³. It is compressed at constant temperature to a volume of 1.2 m³. Calculate the new pressure. (3 marks)
steps: Sense check: volume decreased so pressure increased from 150 to 250 kPa ✓

worked.ans: Model answer: As the tyre warms the air particles gain kinetic energy and move faster. They hit the walls of the tyre more frequently and with a greater force each time. The overall force on each unit of area of the tyre wall increases, so the pressure increases.
worked.q: Explain why the pressure of the air in a sealed car tyre increases when the car has been driven for a long time. The volume of the tyre stays the same. (4 marks)
steps: The temperature of the air rises because the tyre warms up (1).
The particles gain kinetic energy and move faster (1).
They collide with the walls of the tyre more often (1) and with greater force (1).
The force per unit area is greater, so the pressure increases (as volume is constant).
